summary: Ken describes building Harpagia, a free-to-play idle mobile RPG, alongside a full-time tech job and later leaving Meta after Reddit posts brought a sharp increase in revenue. He says the game earns through optional in-app purchases, with average monthly revenue around $13,000 and no ad spend. He built it with a small software stack and used Reddit, player feedback, and freelance creative work to grow and improve it. His main advice is to launch early, learn from potential customers, and prioritize retention before monetization.

ideas.name: Harpagia idle mobile RPG
ideas.one_liner: A free-to-play, text-based incremental RPG where players collect resources and progress while away, with optional in-app purchases.
ideas.business_model: Free-to-play mobile game monetized through optional in-app purchases for premium features or faster progression.
ideas.customer: Fans of incremental and idle RPG games.
ideas.problem: Players want to make meaningful progress while away from the game, then return to collect rewards and choose what to do next.
ideas.offer: A text-based mobile game with skills, resource gathering, upgrades, combat, monsters, loot, and character progression.

pricing.model: Free download with optional one-off in-app purchases.

pricing.notes: Purchases unlock premium features or speed progression. The game is free to play.

acquisition_channels.details: Organic Reddit posts were Ken's main marketing tactic. He shared screenshots, explained the game and its free-to-play approach, and posted major updates every few months because many subreddits limit developer promotion. He reports that posts often brought new players, including posts that drew criticism.

quote.text: Almost every single time that I posted on there, I'd receive a significant jump in new players.
quote.speaker: Ken

acquisition_channels.details: The game is available on iOS and Android. The transcript does not say how many players discovered it through either store.

ideas.delivery: Players access the game as a free-to-play mobile app on iOS and Android. The software runs idle combat and progression, while Ken builds and updates the product. He uses Discord Nitro for community management and freelancers for screenshots, icons, and videos.
unit_economics_claims: In-app purchases are stated to range from $2 to $10, with $4.99 to $9.99 described as a more comfortable range for players.
Ken says revenue per active user averaged over $3 during the past year.
Ken reports average monthly revenue around $13,000 and over $150,000 in revenue during the past year.
Ken reports 3,500 to 4,000 monthly active users and around 5,600 daily active users; the transcript includes a dollar sign before the daily active user figure.
The transcript says the game reached over 50,000 combined across iOS and Android, but does not make clear what that figure measures.
Ken reports a roughly 6% conversion rate and cites 2% to 5% as typical for games.
Ken reports ongoing operating expenses of roughly $500 per month and zero ad spend.
Ken says his first sale was $10, first-month sales were about $150, and total sales by the end of the second month were about $1,500.
Ken says monthly revenue rose from roughly $1,000 to $10,000 after one Reddit post, later reaching a peak around $18,000 per month.
Ken says a small audience of a few hundred active users can generate over $100,000 in annual revenue.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Ken reports ongoing operating expenses of roughly $500 per month, including assets, freelance art, and subscriptions.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Ken says he made his first sale a few days after launch.

acquisition.how: Agents could help draft posts and review feedback, but effective Reddit participation requires human judgment, community-specific rule checks, and responses to players. Ken posted only occasionally because some subreddits limit promotion.

onboarding.how: App download and access can be handled by the platforms. The transcript does not describe account setup, tutorials, or onboarding workflows.

delivery.how: The game and its idle progression are software delivered through mobile apps. Gameplay can run without a person delivering each session; product development and updates still require work.

billing.how: In-app purchases are processed through the mobile game platforms. Ken describes optional purchases but does not specify payment operations.

support.how: Ken uses Discord Nitro for community management. Agents could answer routine questions, but player feedback, complaints, and game issues need human review.

uk_applicability.notes: A mobile game distributed on iOS and Android can serve UK players. The transcript gives no UK-specific localization or operating details.

risks: Subreddits may restrict how often developers can promote a product, limiting posting frequency.
Reddit responses can be strongly critical; Ken says criticism generated discussion, but the transcript does not establish that this will work for every game.
Ken says purchases above $9.99 are harder to convert.
The business depends on ongoing product quality and player retention; Ken says he prioritized retention before monetization.
The transcript's figures for daily active users and the combined iOS/Android total are unclear and may reflect Whisper transcription errors.
The game requires continued development and updates, which limits the extent to which the founder can leave it unattended.

tactics.name: Use Reddit posts to get early players and feedback
steps: Post screenshots and explain what the game is, including its free-to-play approach.
Share major updates every few months when subreddit rules restrict developer promotion.
Treat critical discussion as feedback and engage with the conversation.
Track whether posts lead to new players and revenue.

quote.text: The very first post that I made just showed some screenshots of the game and kind of just explaining a little bit about what the game is and a few metrics about, you know, how to free to play it is
quote.speaker: Ken

tactics.name: Launch early and learn from potential customers
steps: Set a launch deadline; Ken chose to launch after six months regardless of whether the larger vision was complete.
Put the product in front of potential customers or playtesters, not only friends and family.
Use feedback to shape the product and improve later versions.

quote.text: One of the best decisions I made was forcing myself to launch the game after six months, no matter what.
quote.speaker: Ken

tactics.name: Prioritize retention before monetization
steps: Build a game people want to keep playing before focusing on monetization.
Use early player feedback to improve the experience.

quote.text: I also didn't worry much about monetization in the beginning. My focus was retention first and building a game that people wanted to keep playing.
quote.speaker: Ken

tactics.name: Experiment with in-app purchase prices
steps: Test different purchase prices rather than assuming a price will convert.
Ken says players were generally comfortable around $4.99 to $9.99 and that higher prices were harder to convert.

quote.text: What I've learned through a lot of monetization experimentation is anything around $4.99 to $9.99. Players will generally be okay to spend.

tactics.name: Use asset stores and freelancers to save build time
steps: Buy pre-packaged game assets from Unity Asset Store or GameDev Market.
Hire freelancers through Fiverr or Upwork for screenshots, icons, and videos.
Keep the founder focused on building the game.

quote.text: For purchasing assets, I use Unity Asset Store or Game Dev Market, which have a lot of pre-packaged assets that you can purchase and save a lot of time on making part.
quote.speaker: Ken

tactics.name: Start with a small project to learn the full shipping process
steps: Choose a project with a small enough scope to finish quickly.
Use the first build to learn AI-assisted development, product delivery, store approvals, and launch operations.
Apply those lessons to the next project.

quote.text: I also wanted to make sure that the scope was small enough for me to complete in a short amount of time to gain experience of actually shipping something.
quote.speaker: Ken
